title: Learner Data Protection in Kenya: School Software Guide
h1: Learner Data Protection in Kenya: School Software Guide
description: What Kenyan schools must know about learner data protection, from the Data Protection Act 2019 to role-based access and backups in your school software.
primaryKeyword: learner data protection Kenya school software
author: SQUL Team
intro: Every school in Kenya holds a large amount of personal data about children and their families. If you are choosing [school management software in Kenya](/blog/best-school-management-software-kenya), that data is one of the main things you are being trusted with — so it belongs in the buying decision, not in the small print.

This guide translates Kenya's Data Protection Act 2019 into school decisions: what counts as personal data, who is the data controller and who is the processor, what to ask a vendor, and what to insist on before you sign.

sections.heading: Why learner data protection matters to Kenyan schools now

blocks.text: A school holds names, ages, admission numbers, birth certificates, guardian phone numbers, fee balances, health notes, and assessment records. Much of that is sensitive, and almost all of it identifies a child. That is precisely the kind of data the Data Protection Act 2019 was written to protect.

**What counts as personal data in a school.** Anything that identifies a learner or their family: names, contacts, admission and assessment records, fee balances, photos, and health or discipline notes. Special categories — such as health data — attract extra care.

**Paper files, phones, and spreadsheets — where exposure actually happens.** A locked cabinet is reasonably safe. The real risk is the shadow copy: the Excel register emailed between staff, the class list in a teacher's personal phone, the fee book on a laptop that leaves the compound. Digitising without controls simply moves the risk.

sections.heading: Kenya's Data Protection Act 2019 in plain terms

blocks.text: The Data Protection Act 2019 governs how personal data about people in Kenya is collected and used, and it created the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (ODPC) to oversee it. At a high level, it asks anyone handling personal data to follow a set of principles:

items: **Lawfulness, fairness, and transparency** — collect data for a lawful reason and be open about it.
**Purpose limitation** — use data only for the purpose it was collected for.
**Data minimisation** — collect only what you actually need.
**Accuracy** — keep records correct and up to date.
**Storage limitation** — do not keep data longer than necessary.
**Security** — protect data with appropriate technical and organisational measures.
**Accountability** — be able to show how you comply.

blocks.title: This is not legal advice
blocks.text: This page explains the Act at a high level for school decision-making. It is not legal advice. Confirm your school's specific obligations with a qualified Kenyan lawyer or the ODPC before relying on them.

sections.heading: Who is a data controller vs a data processor (school vs vendor)

blocks.caption: Controller and processor in a school-software relationship
rows: Decides why and how learner and parent data is used
Handles that data only on the school's instructions

blocks.text: In plain terms, the **school is usually the data controller** because it decides what learner data is collected and why. A vendor hosting that data is typically a **data processor**, acting on the school's instructions. This framing is widely used, but it should be confirmed for your specific arrangement, and schools should expect a written data-processing agreement with the vendor.

sections.heading: Rights of learners and parents, and the ODPC

blocks.text: The Act gives data subjects rights that, for a school, usually belong to the parent or guardian acting for a child. At a high level these include the right to be informed, to access data, to have it corrected, to have it erased in some circumstances, to object to certain processing, and to lodge a complaint with the ODPC.

**The ODPC** is the regulator. It publishes guidance, handles complaints, and is the body schools register with and turn to when something goes wrong. For children's data, breach notification, registration requirements, and any limits on sending personal data outside Kenya, the details matter — and they change as regulations and guidance evolve.

blocks.title: Specifics to verify
blocks.text: Confirm before relying on them: the children's data provisions and whether parental consent is required, breach-notification timelines, registration of data controllers and processors with the ODPC, and any restrictions on transferring personal data outside Kenya. Check the latest ODPC guidance and regulations rather than a blog summary.

sections.heading: What a compliant school management system must do

blocks.text: You do not need to be a lawyer to judge a system — you need to know what good looks like and what to ask. Use this table as a checklist.

blocks.caption: Requirements, what good looks like, and questions for the vendor
rows: Staff see only the learner data their role requires
"Can a class teacher see fee balances? Can the bursar edit marks?"
"How often do you back up, and how do you restore?"
Only fields the school needs are collected
Records can be archived or deleted on a policy
"How do we remove data we no longer need?"
A clear process for reporting and containing an incident

"Can we see who edited a learner's record and when?"

sections.heading: What to ask your software vendor before you sign

items: **"Where does learner data live, and who can access it?"** You want a clear answer about hosting and internal access.
**"Can you show me role-based access in the live product?"** Not a slide — the actual permission screens.
**"How often do you back up, and how do you restore?"** A backup you have never tested is not a backup.
**"What is your breach-notification process?"** You need to know how and when you would be told.
**"Will you sign a data-processing agreement?"** The school is usually the controller; the vendor should accept the processor role.
**"Can we export and delete our data?"** Portability and deletion matter at the end of a contract, not just the start.

blocks.title: Judge the answer, not the badge
blocks.text: A vendor waving the word "certified" is telling you less than one who can show you access controls, a tested backup, and a signed processing agreement. Ask for the specifics.

sections.heading: The bottom line — and your next step

blocks.text: Learner data protection is not a technical detail — it is part of running a school responsibly. Understand the principles, know that your school is most likely the controller, and ask a vendor to show its access controls and backups rather than tell you about them.
For anything specific to your school, seek legal review. Then start free with one term and inspect the controls for yourself before you commit.

faqs.question: Do we need parental consent to store a learner's data?
faqs.answer: The Act sets a high bar for children's data, and parental consent is often involved, but the exact requirement depends on the circumstances and how children's data provisions are applied. Confirm the current position with a qualified lawyer or the ODPC rather than relying on a general rule.

faqs.question: Are we allowed to keep data outside Kenya?
faqs.answer: The Act places conditions on transferring personal data outside Kenya. Whether a particular vendor's hosting is permitted depends on those conditions, so confirm the current rules and the vendor's data locations before you sign.

faqs.question: What should we do if data is exposed?
faqs.answer: Have a plan before it happens. Contain the incident, assess the risk to learners, follow the Act's breach-reporting requirements — including notifying the ODPC where required — and keep a record of what you did. Confirm the current timelines with the ODPC.

faqs.question: Does the school or the vendor own the data?
faqs.answer: The school generally remains the data controller and stays responsible for the learner data, while the vendor processes it on the school's behalf as a processor. That is why a written data-processing agreement matters.
